usage: I wash my face in the morning
세수하다 specifically means washing your face, not your whole body.
I wash my face and go to sleep
examples: I get up and wash my face
A natural way to describe the start of the day.
I washed my face with cold water
A gentle command, e.g. a parent to a child.
nuance: 세수하다 means specifically to wash your face (얼굴), built from the noun 세수 plus 하다. For washing your whole body you use 샤워하다 or 씻다, and for washing hair you use 감다 — Korean splits these by body part. To make it negative, Koreans usually split the noun and verb: 세수 안 해요 sounds more natural than 안 세수해요.
mistakes: Don't use 세수하다 for showering — it only means washing the face; use 샤워하다 for the whole body.

usage: I brush my teeth after eating
양치하다 is the everyday word for brushing your teeth.
I brush my teeth three times a day
하루에 세 번 = 'three times a day'.
examples: I brush my teeth before bed
I brush my teeth and go to school
You shouldn't skip brushing your teeth
양치 안 하면 안 돼요 = 'it's no good if you don't brush'.
nuance: 양치하다 (also said 양치질하다) is the natural daily word for brushing your teeth, from the noun 양치 plus 하다. You can also say 이를 닦다 (literally 'wash the teeth'), and both are common. As with other 하다 routine verbs, the negative usually splits as 양치 안 해요 rather than 안 양치해요.
mistakes: Don't say 이빨을 닦다 in polite speech — 이빨 is a casual/animal word for teeth; use 양치하다 or 이를 닦다.

usage: I take a shower after exercising
샤워하다 = take a shower, from the loanword 샤워 (shower).
examples: I take a shower every morning
I want to take a shower now
I'll shower and then head out
nuance: 샤워하다 means to take a shower, made from the English loanword 샤워 plus 하다. Use it for washing the whole body under running water; for soaking in a tub you'd say 목욕하다 instead. Most of the time you just say 샤워해요, and you split the negative as 샤워 안 해요 rather than 안 샤워해요.
mistakes: Don't use 샤워하다 for soaking in a bathtub — that's 목욕하다; 샤워하다 is for washing under running water.

usage: I wash the dishes after eating
설거지하다 covers washing all the dishes after a meal.
A polite way to offer to do the dishes.
examples: I washed the dishes after dinner
I don't feel like doing the dishes today
Shall we do the dishes together?
nuance: 설거지하다 is the everyday word for washing dishes after a meal, from the noun 설거지 plus 하다. Note the spelling: it is 설거지 (not 설겆이), one of the trickier native words to write. Like other chore verbs, split the negative as 설거지 안 해요, and you'll often hear it offered politely as 설거지는 제가 할게요.
mistakes: Watch the spelling — it's 설거지, not 설겆이 or 설겆지.

usage: I wash these clothes by hand
I washed the blanket on the weekend
Used for laundering bigger items too.
examples: Please wash this in cold water
A care instruction you'll see on tags.
nuance: 세탁하다 means to launder or wash clothes, from the Sino-Korean noun 세탁 plus 하다. It feels a touch more formal or instructional than the everyday 빨래하다, so you'll see 세탁 on washing machines, laundry tags, and dry-cleaner signs (세탁소 = laundromat/cleaner's). For casual 'I'm doing the laundry' speech, 빨래해요 is just as common.
mistakes: Don't confuse 세탁소 (the laundry shop) with the act 세탁하다 — the shop is the place, the verb is the action.

english: to tidy up / to put in order
usage: 정돈하다 = arrange things neatly into place.
I lined up the shoes neatly
examples: I tidy my room nice and clean
I put the documents in order
nuance: 정돈하다 means to put things in neat order — straightening, lining up, and arranging items into place. It overlaps with 정리하다, but 정돈하다 leans toward making things look tidy and orderly, while 정리하다 leans toward sorting out and clearing away. You'll often see them together as the set phrase 정리정돈 ('tidying and ordering').
mistakes: 정돈하다 is about arranging neatly, not throwing things away — to clear/sort out, 정리하다 fits better.

usage: 꾸미다 = make a space look nice.
꾸미다 also means dressing yourself up.
examples: I decorate the house at Christmas
Decorating a place for an event.
My sister decorated her room prettily
Past tense about a finished result.
I want to dress up a bit for the date
nuance: 꾸미다 covers both decorating a space (방을 꾸미다) and dressing yourself up to look nice (예쁘게 꾸미다). It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so 꾸미 + 어 contracts to 꾸며 → 꾸며요, past 꾸몄어요. The thing you decorate takes 을/를, and you often add an adverb like 예쁘게 ('prettily') or 멋있게 ('stylishly').
mistakes: The polite form is 꾸며요 (꾸미 + 어 → 꾸며), not 꾸미어요.

usage: 감다 is the specific verb for washing hair; the object is 머리.
I wash my hair every day
examples: I washed my hair in the morning
I wash my hair and dry it
I don't feel like washing my hair today
nuance: 감다 is the dedicated verb for washing hair, and it almost always takes 머리 as its object (머리를 감다). Korean uses different verbs by body part: 감다 for hair, 씻다 for hands/body, 세수하다 for the face. It is a regular consonant-stem verb, so 감 + 아요 → 감아요. Note that an identical-looking 감다 also means 'to close (the eyes)', so context tells them apart.
mistakes: Don't say 머리를 씻다 — hair uses 감다, not 씻다.

usage: 말리다 = dry something; here the object is 머리.
examples: I dried my hair with a hair dryer
I dry the towel in the sunlight
I want to dry my wet shoes
nuance: 말리다 means to dry something out — hair, laundry, or wet shoes — and it takes 을/를 for the thing you dry. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 말리 + 어 → 말려요, past 말렸어요. Be aware that the same form 말리다 can also mean 'to stop/talk someone out of something', so context matters; for a beginner, the 'dry' meaning is the one to anchor first.
mistakes: The polite form is 말려요 (말리 + 어), not 말리어요.

english: to apply / to put on (cream, etc.)
usage: 바르다 = spread/apply something onto skin or a surface.
Be sure to put on sunscreen
examples: I wash my face and put on lotion
I spread jam on the bread
바르다 also works for spreading food.
I apply medicine to the wound
nuance: 바르다 means to apply or spread something onto a surface — lotion, sunscreen, jam, or ointment. It is a 르-irregular verb: before -아/어 the 르 drops and an extra ㄹ appears, giving 발라요 and past 발랐어요 (never 바르어요). The thing applied takes 을/를, and the surface takes 에 (얼굴에 로션을 발라요).
mistakes: Because it's 르-irregular, the past is 발랐어요, not 바르었어요.

usage: 빗다 = comb/brush the hair; object is 머리.
I comb my hair with a comb
빗으로 = 'with a comb' (the noun 빗 = comb).
examples: I comb my hair in the morning
Please comb your hair a bit
A light suggestion to tidy up.
nuance: 빗다 means to comb or brush your hair, and it takes 머리 as its object. The tool, a comb, is the noun 빗 (so 빗으로 빗다 = 'comb with a comb'). It is a regular consonant-stem verb: 빗 + 어요 → 빗어요, past 빗었어요. Don't mix it up with 씻다 (to wash) — they look and sound similar but mean different things.
mistakes: Don't confuse 빗다 (to comb) with 씻다 (to wash) — they look alike but are different verbs.

usage: I wake my younger sibling in the morning
깨우다 = wake someone else up (takes a person as object).
A useful request, e.g. at a guesthouse.
examples: A request to let someone sleep.
nuance: 깨우다 is the transitive 'wake someone up', so it takes a person as its object (저를 깨워요). It is the causative pair of 깨다 (to wake up by oneself) and of 일어나다 (to get up). The stem ends in 우, so 우 + 어 contracts to 워, giving 깨워요 and past 깨웠어요. The phrase 깨워 주세요 ('please wake me') is handy when staying somewhere overnight.
mistakes: Use 깨우다 to wake SOMEONE ELSE; to say you yourself wake up, use 일어나다 or 깨다.

usage: I rinse the dish with water
헹구다 = rinse off with clean water.
Used at the dentist or after brushing.
examples: I wash the dishes and rinse them clean
Follows 설거지하다 in the dish routine.
I rinsed the vegetables under running water
I rinse the laundry one more time
nuance: 헹구다 means to rinse something with clean water to get the soap or dirt off — dishes, vegetables, laundry, or your mouth. The object takes 을/를 and the water often takes 에/로. The stem ends in 우, so 우 + 어 contracts to 궈, giving 헹궈요 and past 헹궜어요. It naturally follows 씻다 or 설거지하다 as the 'final clean-water step'.
mistakes: The polite form is 헹궈요 (헹구 + 어 → 헹궈), not 헹구어요 or 헹궈어요.
